messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
For a simple “projectile‑motion” model (no friction, constant gravity \(g\), flat ground) the **horizontal** distance travelled after a time \(t\) is obtained directly from the component of the launch velocity parallel to the ground:

\[
x(t)=v\,\cos(\theta)\;\times\;t .
\]

---

### Why this works  
* The launch velocity vector \((v_x,v_y)\) splits into:
  - Horizontal component \(v_x=v\cos\theta\)
  - Vertical component \(v_y=v\sin\theta\)

* In uniform–gravity flight the horizontal acceleration is zero, so the horizontal speed stays constant at \(v_x\).

* Distance covered horizontally during a time interval \(t\) equals speed × time → \(x=t\,v_x\).

If you also care about vertical displacement,
\[
y(t)=v\,\sin(\theta)\,t-\frac12 g t^{2},
\]
but the question asked only for how far the car travels along the ground.

---

#### Quick sanity checks  

| Parameter | Value | Result |
|-----------|-------|--------|
| \(v=20~{\rm m/s}\) | \(\theta=30^\circ\) | \(x=\!20\times\!\cos30^\circ\times1≈17.32~m\) per second |
| \(v=50~{\rm km/h}=13.89~{\rm m/s}\) | \(\theta=45^\circ\) | \(x=13.89/\sqrt{2}\approx9.82~m/t\) |

So, simply multiply the launch speed’s horizontal component by the elapsed time.

> **Tip:** If you’re coding this in JavaScript/TypeScript, here’s a tiny helper:

```ts
function horizontalDistance(v: number, θDeg: number, t: number): number {
    const rad = θDeg * Math.PI / 180;
    return v * Math.cos(rad) * t;
}
```

Feel free to plug your numbers in—just remember that real cars won’t follow perfect projectile dynamics because of rolling resistance, engine torque limits, etc., but for a quick estimate this gives the right order of magnitude.
